title: Philemon 1:1
content:
Section 1–3: Paulos (Paul) and Timotheos (Timothy) greet Filemon (Philemon)

When Christians in New Testament times wrote a letter, they usually started by doing three things. First they wrote the name of the person or people who were writing the letter. Then they wrote the name of the person or people who would be receiving the letter. Then they wrote a Christian greeting. Paulos did all three things in his letter to Filemon. He included:

  • The name of the person who wrote the letter: Paulos (verse 1)

  • The name of the person receiving the letter: Filemon (verse 1)

  • A Christian greeting (verse 3)

Your translation may be easier to read if each of these three parts is a separate paragraph, as in the GNT, BSB, NIV, and RSV versions.

Carefully consider the best way to arrange the information in verses 1–3 when you translate verses 1–3. What is the usual way to begin a letter in your language? Can you follow that style and still include the three parts from Paulos’s opening Section? All of the information in this opening Section should also be in the opening Section of your translation. For example, do not take Paulos’s name out of the opening paragraph even though writers in your language put their name at the end of the letter. After you have decided what is the best way to begin a letter in your language, follow that same basic way consistently in your translations of all of Paulos’s letters.

Read verses 1–3 carefully in the BSB and the GNT. Then read the following notes and the Display before you begin to translate.

1a

Paulos (Paul), a prisoner of Christ Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus),

  • ¶ This letter is from me, Paulos. I am in prison because I preach about Yeshua Christ.

Paulos: The apostle Paulos wrote this letter. He began by writing his name. There is no verb in verse 1 in the Greek text. But many languages require complete sentences, so you may need to add a verb. Paulos was writing a letter to Filemon (Philemon), so you could use a form of the verb “write” or the verb “greet.”

It is not natural in some languages for someone to talk about himself in the third person. For example, it would not be correct in some languages for Paulos to write, “Paulos is writing to you.” In such cases, you could translate this in a first person form:

I, Paulos, am writing this letter.

a prisoner of Christ Yeshua: Paulos was saying, “I am in prison because I do the work of Christ Yeshua.” GNT: “A prisoner for the sake of Christ Yeshua.” Paulos was in prison when he wrote this letter. But that was not because he did something wrong. People put him in prison because he preached the Good News about Yeshua Christ. Those who didn’t believe in Yeshua Christ didn’t like Paulos’s message, and so they put him in prison.

Christ Yeshua: Paulos and other authors who wrote New Testament books usually wrote “Yeshua Christ” as Paulos did in verse 3, instead of the name Christ Yeshua, which Paulos wrote here. The meaning is the same either way. If people who read your translation will think that Christ Yeshua is a different person from “Yeshua Christ,” you should use the more common order “Yeshua Christ” here also.

1b

and Timotheos (Timothy) our brother, To Filemon

  • I and our(incl) fellow believer Timotheos greet you, Filemon.

  • Greetings to you, Filemon, from our Christian brother Timotheos and from me.

Timotheos: Timotheos also sent Filemon (Philemon) his greetings. Timotheos was Paulos’s (Paul’s) close friend who worked for Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) just as Paulos did. Bible scholars think that Timotheos probably did not help Paulos write this letter. But he was with Paulos at the time Paulos wrote the letter, and he also wanted to greet Filemon.

brother: The word brother in this context refers to a fellow believer in Christ. Paulos, Timotheos and Filemon were probably not physically related to each other as members of the same earthly family are. Timotheos was a younger Christian, a fellow believer of Paulos and also of Filemon and the other Christians at Kolossai (Colosse).

The word brother as used among Christians means that they are spiritual brothers and sisters because they are God’s children. They are closely related to one another in this sense. Perhaps you can use the term “brother” for men who are Christians and “sister” for women who are Christians (as in verse 2). Or perhaps there is a word that you could use to include both men and women (such as “sibling” in English). If your language has different words for “older brother” and “younger brother,” use “younger brother” here in verse 1 because Timotheos was younger than both Paulos and Filemon. If “brother” means only a member of the same family in your language and no one will understand a spiritual relationship here, a footnote could explain how Christians used the term then. Or perhaps there may be another term you can use to show how one family member is related to another family member.

To Filemon: This means “We greet you, Filemon.” This was a way people wrote letters in Paulos’s time. Filemon, who received the letter, understood the implied meaning “we send greetings.”

Filemon: Filemon was the main person Paulos was writing this letter to. Filemon, who lived in the town of Kolossai, was an important man and was probably rich. He was also the master of the slave Onesimos (Onesimus). Paulos had helped Filemon to become a Christian (see verse 19b).

1c

our beloved fellow worker,

  • You are a dear friend and you work for Christ like we(dual excl) do.

our beloved: Both Paulos and Timotheos (Timothy) loved Filemon very much. You could translate the phrase our beloved as “We love you very much.” See Display for verse 1c.

fellow worker: The phrase fellow worker means that Filemon helped to spread the Good News, like Paulos and Timotheos did. He probably did not work together with Paulos in the same place.

Read verses 1–3 carefully in the BSB and the GNT. Then read the following notes and the Display before you begin to translate.

2

to Apfia (Apphia)…Arkippos (Archippus)…the church: Paulos (Paul) included these people’s names in the list of the people he was greeting, but he wrote the letter mainly to Filemon (Philemon). Beginning at verse 4, Paulos wrote directly to Filemon. Even if your translation addresses Filemon in the second person (“to you, Filemon”), perhaps you should refer to these people in the third person. For example, “We send greetings to Apfia…,” or “Give our greetings to Apfia….”

2a

to Apfia our sister,

  • We(dual excl) also greet Apfia, who is our(incl) fellow believer.

  • Greetings to Apfia, who is like a sister to us.(incl)

sister: Paulos also greeted Apfia. The phrase “Apfia our sister” means that Apfia was a believer in Christ as Paulos was. She did not have the same father or mother as Paulos and Filemon. See the note on “brother” in verse 1b.

2b

to Arkippos our fellow soldier,

  • We(dual excl) also greet Arkippos, who strongly preaches the Good News with us.(incl)

fellow soldier: Paulos (Paul) also greeted Arkippos (Archippus). The phrase Arkippos our fellow soldier implies that Arkippos spoke out bravely for Christ when people were against the Good News, like a soldier fights to protect his country. (Colossians 4:17, 1 John 2:14) But there is nothing to indicate that Arkippos was a soldier in any earthly army.

2c

and to the church that meets at your house:

  • We(dual excl) also greet the other Christians who worship God at your house.

church: Paulos also greeted the believers that met in Filemon’s (Philemon’s) house. They met together with Filemon regularly to worship the Lord. Christians didn’t have church buildings in those days. They met in homes. See “church", sense 1 in Key Biblical Terms.

your house: This refers to Filemon’s home.

Read verses 1–3 carefully in the BSB and the GNT. Then read the following notes and the Display before you begin to translate.

3

Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ.

  • May God our(incl) Father and Yeshua Christ our Lord bless you(plur) and cause you to have peace in your hearts.

Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Yeshua Christ: Many Christians greeted one another in this way (verse 3) in the early days of Christianity. It is as if Paulos (Paul) was saying a prayer, asking God to bless those he was writing to.

Grace and peace: This was a greeting and blessing Paulos often used in his letters. (For example, 1 Corinthians 1:3, Galatians 1:3, Ephesians 1:2).

Grace: The word Grace in this context means “kindness, favor, good will, or blessing.” Paulos was asking God to be kind to those to whom he was writing. He wanted God to favor them. Try to think of ways in your language for asking God to bless someone. The term Grace is an important term in the New Testament. See “grace", sense A2(b) in Key Biblical Terms.

peace: Paulos meant “peace of heart” here. This results from a person having peace with God. The term peace also implies “peace with one another.” People who have peace of heart normally live in peace with one another.

to you: The word you is plural here and thus includes all the people whom Paulos addressed in the first two verses.

God our Father: For Christians, God is like a father, one who loves us and cares for us.

Lord: The word Lord here in verse 3 means “master” or “leader.” Yeshua Christ is our spiritual leader. We who are Christians should obey him as a servant obeys his master. See “Christ", sense 4 in Key Biblical Terms .

title: Philemon 1:4
content:
Section 4–7: Paulos (Paul) thanks God for Filemon (Philemon) and prays for him

After Paulos greeted Filemon and his friends, Paulos thanked God for him and prayed for him. This is the way he started most of his letters. For other examples, see Philippians 1:3–11 and Colossians 1:3–14. Before he asked Filemon to do something, Paulos wanted to tell Filemon how much he loved and respected him. Paulos thanked God because Filemon had faith in the Lord Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), and because he loved God’s people. This love gave Paulos great joy. And Paulos prayed that Filemon’s fellowship with other believers would increase and deepen because he (Filemon) knows the good things that God has given believers.

In this Section Paulos wrote directly to Filemon. He used only “you (sing)” in verses 4–21, not “you (plur)” as he did in the beginning and end of the letter.

Read verses 4–7 carefully in the BSB and the GNT, and then read the following notes before translating.

4

I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers,

  • ¶ Whenever I pray for you, I always thank God, whom I worship, for you.

  • ¶ Whenever I pray for you, I always thank God for you—the God whom I worship.

Verse 4 could have one of two meanings:

  1. Every time I pray for you I thank God (for you) (NIV, NCV, CEV, RSV, NLT). This means that Paulos (Paul) did not thank God for Filemon (Philemon) every time he prayed.

  2. Every time I pray I thank God for you. (GNT, KJV, JBP, JB). This means that Paulos did thank God for Filemon every time he prayed.

The first meaning is probably what Paulos intended.

my God: This means “The God I know and belong to and worship.” Paulos related to God in a very personal way. But a literal translation of the phrase “my God” may imply a wrong meaning in some languages. Check carefully on this point.

remembering: Paulos meant that when he prayed he “mentioned” Filemon to God, he “prayed for” him. Be careful not to use a word that would imply he had forgotten Filemon and then remembered him.

title: Philemon 1:5
content:

After Paulos greeted Filemon and his friends, Paulos thanked God for him and prayed for him. This is the way he started most of his letters. And Paulos prayed that Filemon’s fellowship with other believers would increase and deepen because he (Filemon) knows the good things that God has given believers.

In this Section Paulos wrote directly to Filemon. He used only “you (sing)” in verses 4–21, not “you (plur)” as he did in the beginning and end of the letter.

Read verses 4–7 carefully in the BSB and the GNT, and then read the following notes before translating.

5

because I hear about your faith in the Lord Yeshua and your love for all the saints.

  • I do this because people tell me that you continue to believe in the Lord Yeshua and that you love all of God’s people.

Paulos himself had led Filemon to believe in the Lord Yeshua. So Paulos was thanking God, apparently because people had told him that Filemon continued to trust in the Lord Yeshua and that he loved all God’s people. The word “because” (BSB) shows that the reason Paulos thanked God for Filemon (verse 4) was that Filemon trusted in Christ and loved Christ’s people (verse 5).

In the RSV it is not clear how the words love, faith, Yeshua, and saints go together. In the BSB, NIV and CEV the meaning is clear. For example:

…the faith you have in the Lord Yeshua and the love you have for all God’s people.

your faith in the Lord Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus): You could restate this as “You believe in the Lord Yeshua.”

faith: The word faith means “belief” or “trust.” Paulos (Paul) was glad to hear that Filemon (Philemon) continued to believe that the Lord Yeshua was the Messiah. And Filemon trusted the Lord Yeshua to save him from the punishment for sinning and to give him power not to sin.

your love for all the saints: Using an active verb expresses this more clearly: “You love all the saints.”

love: The Greek word agapē here refers to one person loving another or others. Filemon truly loved God’s people.

saints: The Greek word hagious (literally “holy ones”) in this verse refers to Christians, those who belong to God. See “holy", sense A3(a) in Key Biblical Terms.

title: Philemon 1:6
content:
Section 4–7: Paulos (Paul) thanks God for Filemon (Philemon) and prays for him

After Paulos greeted Filemon and his friends, Paulos thanked God for him and prayed for him. This is the way he started most of his letters. For other examples, see Philippians 1:3–11 and Colossians 1:3–14. Before he asked Filemon to do something, Paulos wanted to tell Filemon how much he loved and respected him. Paulos thanked God because Filemon had faith in the Lord Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), and because he loved God’s people. This love gave Paulos great joy. And Paulos prayed that Filemon’s fellowship with other believers would increase and deepen because he (Filemon) knows the good things that God has given believers.

In this Section Paulos wrote directly to Filemon. He used only “you (sing)” in verses 4–21, not “you (plur)” as he did in the beginning and end of the letter.

Read verses 4–7 carefully in the BSB and the GNT, and then read the following notes before translating.

6

I pray that your partnership in the faith may become effective as you fully acknowledge every good thing that is ours in Christ.

  • I pray that the fellowship which you have with those, who believe as you do, may increase/deepen, through your knowing all the good things that God has given us.(incl) May this happen for the glory of Christ.

  • I pray that the fellowship which you have with those people who believe in Christ as you believe in him would increase and deepen. I pray that this would be the result of your learning about all the good things that God has given us.(incl) I want this to happen for the glory of Christ.

  • I pray that you may fellowship more and more with those who believe, and that you may know all the good things that God has given us.(incl) I pray this so that people will honor Christ.

(Literal Greek translation:) that the sharing of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing in us in Christ: There are various ways to interpret this verse and, as a result, different English versions have translated it differently.

The interpretation of the first part of the verse depends on several interrelated questions:

How is the word koinōnia “fellowship, sharing” to be understood?

Who are the participants in each event? That is, with whom is Filemon (Philemon) sharing in believing? Is it with other Christians (later including Onesimos (Onesimus)) or is it with Paulos (Paul) (and Timotheos (Timothy))?

What is the connection between “may become active” and “in/by knowledge”? Does the phrase “in the knowledge of every good thing” describe the means by which that fellowship or sharing becomes effectual, or is the knowledge of every good thing the result of that fellowship/sharing?

Here are three alternative interpretations that seem the most likely, out of several possibilities that commentators have suggested:

  1. That sharing (Greek: koinōnia) refers to sharing, or bonding, with others who believe the same truths. English Bible versions often translate koinōnia as “fellowship” when it has this sense. In this interpretation the meaning is that Paulos was praying that Filemon would have active fellowship with other believers as he came to understand every good thing that God had done for (or in) God’s people. In this interpretation the words “in the knowledge of every good thing” refer to the means by which this fellowship or bonding would happen. This fits well with the theme of the letter. Paulos was about to appeal to Filemon to be merciful toward his runaway slave, Onesimos, because now they both believed in Christ. Although Paulos had not yet mentioned his request to Filemon to forgive Onesimos, he was looking forward to the fellowship that Filemon would have with Onesimos. This would happen because they both now recognized God’s goodness to them.

  2. That Sharing means that Filemon shared his faith with others, that is, he told other people about the gospel message he believed. (NIV and CEV follow this interpretation.) So the phrase “in the knowledge of every good thing” could refer to the result of sharing his faith. There is more than one way to interpret what this result might be. NIV interprets this to mean that Paulos prayed that, as Filemon told others about what he believed, Filemon would gain “a full understanding of every good thing we have in Christ.” CEV interprets this to mean that Paulos prays that as Filemon tells others about what he believes, those people “will come to know all the blessing Christ has given believers.”

  3. That Sharing means “fellowship” as in the first interpretation, but here in verse 6 it is the fellowship Paulos and Timotheos had with Filemon that is in focus. The words “in the knowledge of every good thing” refer to the results of Filemon’s fellowship with Paulos and Timotheos. Thus GNT interprets the meaning of Paulos’s prayer to be that, as Filemon had fellowship with Paulos and Timotheos, Filemon would understand more deeply all the blessings they had as they lived in union with Christ.

There are also other possible interpretations of this verse. However, the first interpretation seems to fit best with the purpose of the letter. Paulos was preparing Filemon for something he was about to ask Filemon to do on behalf of their fellow believer, Onesimos. Paulos was probably thinking about how Filemon could help Onesimos. He was preparing Filemon by asking him to think about the good things God had given all Christians and by urging him to act for Christ’s honor. Remembering these facts would cause Filemon to have closer fellowship with all Christians, including his slave, Onesimos, who had recently become a Christian.

There is yet another problem that you need to consider. Different versions translate the Greek phrase eis Christon at the end of the verse (among other ways) as “in Christ,” “for Christ,” or “to Christ.” There are two interpretations of how the word eis functions in this verse:

  1. The Greek word eis relates to the Greek verb that the literal English version above translates “become effective.” This would mean that the purpose for becoming effective is to honor Christ. If you agree with this interpretation, you might restate the phrase in Christ this way: “May this happen for the sake of Christ,” or “This will bring honor to Christ,” or “This will cause people to praise Christ.” JB, NASB and the Amplified Bible follow this interpretation (1).

  2. The Greek word eis relates to the phrase “every good thing.” Thus the whole phrase would imply “all the good things that are ours because we are in union with Christ,” or “because we believe in Christ.” The BSB, NIV and GNT follow this interpretation (2).

There is also a textual problem in this verse. In place of en hēmin ‘in us,’ some ancient Greek manuscripts have en humin ‘in you.’ However the weight of the manuscript evidence seems to support en hēmin. Also the UBS Greek New Testament 4th edition rates this reading as a B (very probable) degree of certainty. Of the major English versions, only the KJV and the NASB follow the reading en humin.

The Display (first Meaning Line) for verse 6 shows a translation of verse 6 that follows interpretation (1) above:

I pray that the fellowship which you have with those who believe as you do may increase/deepen, through your knowing all the good things that God has given us (incl). May this happen for the glory of Christ.

The notes on “fellowship", sense A2 in Key Biblical Terms support this interpretation

Or, if you choose interpretation (2) above for verse 6, you could translate the whole verse as follows:

I pray that you may be active in sharing your faith, so that you will come to understand fully all the good things God has given us(incl), and that this will result in people glorifying Christ.

title: Philemon 1:7
content:
Section 4–7: Paulos (Paul) thanks God for Filemon (Philemon) and prays for him

After Paulos greeted Filemon and his friends, Paulos thanked God for him and prayed for him. This is the way he started most of his letters. For other examples, see Philippians 1:3–11 and Colossians 1:3–14. Before he asked Filemon to do something, Paulos wanted to tell Filemon how much he loved and respected him. Paulos thanked God because Filemon had faith in the Lord Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), and because he loved God’s people. This love gave Paulos great joy. And Paulos prayed that Filemon’s fellowship with other believers would increase and deepen because he (Filemon) knows the good things that God has given believers.

In this Section Paulos wrote directly to Filemon. He used only “you (sing)” in verses 4–21, not “you (plur)” as he did in the beginning and end of the letter.

Read verses 4–7 carefully in the BSB and the GNT, and then read the following notes before translating.

7a

I take great joy and encouragement in your love,

  • I am very happy and encouraged because you love others!

  • The way that you love others has caused me to be very happy and has encouraged me.

Some translations use a connecting word at the beginning of this verse to show that verse 7 is another reason why Paulos thanked God. See also verse 4. For example:

For (RSV)

your love: Filemon (Philemon) was showing that he loved God’s people. This refers to the love that Paulos (Paul) thanked God for in verse 5.

encouragement: When Filemon showed that he loved God’s people, it helped to strengthen Paulos’s ability to trust God and it helped to comfort him while he was in prison.

7b

because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints.

  • You, my fellow believer, have encouraged God’s people!

because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints: Paulos was very happy because Filemon had caused God’s people to be happy.

because: Paulos was thinking about a specific way that Filemon had showed God’s people that he loved them when he mentioned Filemon’s love in 7a. Verse 7b explains what specific way of showing love Paulos was thinking about in 7a.

brother: See the note on verse 1b.

refreshed: (GNT:) “cheered.” This means when someone causes someone else to rest, to feel better, to be happy, to have new courage, to be encouraged.

the hearts of the saints: This refers to the way God’s people felt in their inner selves, in their souls.

General Comment on 1:7

Here are two different ways to translate verse 7:

My brother, you love God’s people and you have made them happy. This gives me great joy and comfort.

Brother, you love your fellow believers there and it causes me to feel great joy. It has also strengthened my faith because you have caused God’s people to be happy.

title: Philemon 1:8
content:
Section 8–21: Paulos (Paul) asks Filemon (Philemon) to accept back Onesimos (Onesimus), Filemon’s runaway slave

This is the main part of the letter. Paulos stated clearly in verse 17 what he was asking Filemon to do. He said, “Welcome Onesimos back just as you would welcome me.” But before Paulos asked Filemon to do this, he told Filemon several reasons why he should welcome Onesimos back. In verses 8–11, he told Filemon that he wanted him to do something to help Onesimos because Onesimos had become a Christian and would be useful to Filemon. Paulos told Filemon that another reason why he should help Onesimos was because Filemon loved Paulos and his other Christian brothers. In verses 12–14, Paulos said that he was sending Onesimos back to Filemon, even though he wanted to keep Onesimos with him. In verses 15–16, Paulos told Filemon why God may have allowed these things to happen, and that he (Paulos) loved Onesimos very much. Then in verses 17–21, Paulos finally said clearly that he wanted Filemon to welcome Onesimos. Paulos offered to pay for anything Onesimos owed to Filemon. He also reminded Filemon that in the past he had helped Filemon become a Christian. This was another reason why Paulos expected that Filemon would do what he asked.

In this Section (verses 8–21) Paulos, as a Christian brother, asked Filemon to help Onesimos, but did not command him to do it.

Read verses 8–21 carefully in the BSB and the GNT.

Paragraph 8–11 Paulos appeals to Filemon on behalf of Onesimos

Read verses 8–11 again, then read the following notes before you translate.

8

So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper,

  • ¶ I ask you to do something that you should do. I could use the authority Christ has given me to command you to do this, but I won’t.

  • ¶For this reason I ask you to do the right thing as a Christian. I could be bold as Christ’s apostle and order you to do it.

So: “For this reason” (GNT). This means that the words in verse 7 are the reason for what Paulos (Paul) said in 8–9a. He was thinking like this: Therefore (since Filemon (Philemon) loves his Christian brothers,) he should also love Onesimos (Onesimus). But Paulos did not yet make all of this meaning explicit.

in Christ: There are two ways of understanding the meaning of the phrase in Christ:

  1. As an apostle of Christ, Paulos had authority from Christ to command Filemon to do this.

  2. As a Christian brother, Paulos had a close relationship with Filemon that freed him to tell Filemon to do this. GNT follows this interpretation by translating this “as your brother in Christ.”

The following phrase in the BSB is: I am bold enough to order you . So the first interpretation fits better with this idea of giving an order in contrast to asking him to do something.

bold: The word bold means “not afraid.” Paulos was not afraid to say whatever he should say.

order: To order someone means to command him. It means to tell someone to do something. As an apostle of Christ, Paulos could have told Filemon to help Onesimos. But Paulos decided it was better to ask him, as a friend and a fellow Christian.

to do what is proper: This refers to what Paulos thought Filemon should do in order to act as a Christian should act. What Paulos implied here was that he wanted Filemon to welcome Onesimos. But Paulos did not say this openly until verse 17.

title: Philemon 1:9
content:
Section 8–21: Paulos (Paul) asks Filemon (Philemon) to accept back Onesimos (Onesimus), Filemon’s runaway slave

Read verses 8–11 again, then read the following notes before you translate.

9a

I prefer to appeal on the basis of love.

  • Instead, I am simply asking you to do it because we (dual-incl) love each other and God’s people.

  • But I will only ask you, because I know you love me and your fellow believers.

  2. Filemon should do what he ought to do, not because of a command, but because he loved all of God’s people.

9b

For I, Paulos (Paul), am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) as well.

  • He was an old man.

a prisoner: See notes on verse 1a.

Read verses 8–11 again, then read the following notes before you translate.

10a

I appeal to you for my child Onesimos,

Paulos used these words in verse 11 to encourage Filemon to act favorably toward Onesimos.

Formerly he was useless to you,

  • ¶ I am sending Onesimos (Onesimus) back to you, he whom I love with all my heart.

13

I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel.

  • I wanted to keep him here with me to help me while I am in prison for preaching the Good News about Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ. He could take your place helping me here, because I know that you want to help me.

I would have liked: “I would like” (GNT). You could freely translate the first part of verse 13 as “If I did what I wanted, I would keep him here.” But Paulos (Paul) didn’t do what he wanted to do for himself. He let Filemon (Philemon) decide (verse 14).

14a

But I did not want to do anything without your consent,

  • But I am not keeping him here yet because you have not yet approved.

  • But I don’t want to do it unless you agree.

What Paulos (Paul) meant in this verse was that he did not ask Onesimos (Onesimus) to stay with him, since Filemon (Philemon) was not there to approve of it. If he had asked Onesimos to stay, this would have been like forcing Filemon to let Onesimos help Paulos. But Paulos wanted Filemon to do this only if Filemon himself wanted to do it, not because Paulos said he must do it.

anything: The word anything here means “anything (in this matter about Onesimos).” Paulos would not keep Onesimos with him and would not ask Onesimos to come back (to Paulos) unless Filemon approved.

without your consent: Other ways to express this are “unless you say OK” or “without you saying it is all right.” See Display for verse 14a.

14b

so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will.

  • I desire that any kind thing you do for me will be because you want to do it, not because I forced you to do it.

  • I want your reason for doing any helpful thing for me to be because you want to do it, not because I caused you to do it.

  • In this way, if you do what I ask, it will be because you want to do it, not because you have to.

your goodness: Another way to state this is “If you help me like this….”

goodness: Paulos was referring here to something kind or helpful Filemon (Philemon) might do for him. See “ appeal” in verse 10.

not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will: If Filemon did a favor for Paulos, Paulos wanted it to be something Filemon himself decided to do, not something that Paulos ordered him to do whether Filemon wanted to do it or not.

out of compulsion: When someone makes or compels you to do something, or forces you to some action.

by your own free will: This means “without someone telling you to do it.” To do it willingly because you want to do it.

Paragraph 15–16 Onesimos is now a brother in Christ

15a-b

for a while…for good: (GNT:) “short time…all time” The short time that Onesimos was away from Filemon—perhaps a few months—helped him to return and be with him for all time (on this earth and in heaven) as a fellow Christian. For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while,

  • ¶ It may be that God let Onesimos (Onesimus) run away from you for a short time

perhaps: Paulos (Paul) was not certain that what he said in 15a–16a was God’s plan, but he thought that it was likely.

so that you might have him back for good—

16a

no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.

  • And from now on he will not be merely your slave. He is more than a slave. He is now your dear Christian brother.

  • You should no longer consider him to be only your slave. He is more than a slave. He is now a fellow believer whom you can love.

content:

Read verses 8–21 carefully in the BSB and the GNT.

Paragraph 17–21 Paulos asks Filemon to welcome Onesimos back

In this paragraph Paulos finally stated clearly to Filemon what he wanted him to do. He wanted Filemon to welcome Onesimos back in the same way that Filemon would welcome Paulos if Paulos were visiting him. This is the main point of the whole letter.

Paulos promised to repay Filemon for anything Onesimos may have taken from Filemon or for anything wrong he may have done against him. But Paulos knew that Filemon probably would not ask him to repay him, because Paulos had helped him to become a Christian. Christ surely changed the way Filemon thought about life and about money. In fact, Paulos was sure that Filemon would do what he was asking him to do and even more.

Paulos was also sending Onesimos back to Filemon because Onesimos needed to obey his master again and help him and show that he had changed. If Onesimos did this, he and Filemon could have peace with each other again.

Read verses 17–21 again.

17a

So if you consider me a partner,

  • ¶ So, since you think of me as someone who works with you for Christ,

  • ¶ Therefore, if you think of us (dual-incl) as people who work together,

So: Instead of saying So, Paulos (Paul) could have said “On the basis of what I have just said.” (verses 8–16). This would mean the same thing. He could also have said, “Thinking of what I have just written to you.”

if: Another way of expressing what Paulos means by the word the BSB translates as if is “since” or “because.” Paulos often used the word if with this meaning. If you translated 17a as “I am not sure you consider me a partner,” this would be the wrong meaning. Paulos knew that Filemon (Philemon) thought of him as his partner. So he was saying, “Since you think of me as your partner.”

partner: The Greek word koinōnos in this verse means “a friend who is a fellow Christian” (see verse 17 in LB, JBP). It refers to someone who works together with someone else to serve the Lord. This is very similar to the meaning of the term that the BSB translates as “fellow worker” in verse 1.

17b

receive him as you would receive me.

  • welcome Onesimos (Onesimus) back just as gladly as you would welcome me.

  • when Onesimos comes back to you, treat him as kindly as you would treat me.

receive: To receive someone means to welcome him, to accept him gladly. Paulos was asking Filemon to receive Onesimos back just as gladly as he would have received Paulos.

title: Philemon 1:18
content:
Section 8–21: Paulos (Paul) asks Filemon (Philemon) to accept back Onesimos (Onesimus), Filemon’s runaway slave

This is the main part of the letter. Paulos stated clearly in verse 17 what he was asking Filemon to do. He said, “Welcome Onesimos back just as you would welcome me.” But before Paulos asked Filemon to do this, he told Filemon several reasons why he should welcome Onesimos back. In verses 8–11, he told Filemon that he wanted him to do something to help Onesimos because Onesimos had become a Christian and would be useful to Filemon. Paulos told Filemon that another reason why he should help Onesimos was because Filemon loved Paulos and his other Christian brothers. In verses 12–14, Paulos said that he was sending Onesimos back to Filemon, even though he wanted to keep Onesimos with him. In verses 15–16, Paulos told Filemon why God may have allowed these things to happen, and that he (Paulos) loved Onesimos very much. Then in verses 17–21, Paulos finally said clearly that he wanted Filemon to welcome Onesimos. Paulos offered to pay for anything Onesimos owed to Filemon. He also reminded Filemon that in the past he had helped Filemon become a Christian. This was another reason why Paulos expected that Filemon would do what he asked.

In this Section (verses 8–21) Paulos, as a Christian brother, asked Filemon to help Onesimos, but did not command him to do it.

Read verses 8–21 carefully in the BSB and the GNT.

Paragraph 17–21 Paulos asks Filemon to welcome Onesimos back

In this paragraph Paulos finally stated clearly to Filemon what he wanted him to do. He wanted Filemon to welcome Onesimos back in the same way that Filemon would welcome Paulos if Paulos were visiting him. This is the main point of the whole letter.

Paulos promised to repay Filemon for anything Onesimos may have taken from Filemon or for anything wrong he may have done against him. But Paulos knew that Filemon probably would not ask him to repay him, because Paulos had helped him to become a Christian. Christ surely changed the way Filemon thought about life and about money. In fact, Paulos was sure that Filemon would do what he was asking him to do and even more.

Paulos was also sending Onesimos back to Filemon because Onesimos needed to obey his master again and help him and show that he had changed. If Onesimos did this, he and Filemon could have peace with each other again.

Read verses 17–21 again.

18

But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account.

  • If he has done anything bad against you or if he owes you any money, let me pay for it.

  • If Onesimos (Onesimus) has wronged you or is in debt to you for anything, I will pay it.

It is not clear whether Onesimos did anything wrong except run away. But remember, Filemon (Philemon) was his master. Onesimos belonged to him. He did not have to pay Onesimos to work for him. When Onesimos ran away, Filemon may have had to hire another worker and pay him. So he may have felt that Onesimos owed him the money that he had had to pay the other worker. Onesimos may also have stolen something from Filemon, but Bible scholars are not certain about this.

owes: He needed to repay something to Filemon.

charge it to my account: This does not refer to a bank account. Paulos (Paul) did not have any kind of financial account with Filemon. Paulos was saying, “Whatever Onesimos owes you, don’t say he owes it but say I owe it to you.” Paulos was promising to repay to Filemon anything that Onesimos owed him. But the next two verses give reasons why Filemon would probably not let Paulos repay him.

19a

I, Paulos, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—

  • I am writing this in my own handwriting: “I, Paulos (Paul), will pay you anything Onesimos (Onesimus) owes you.”

Bible scholars do not know if Paulos wrote the rest of this letter with his own hand or if he only wrote this part. It seems that normally Paulos dictated his letters to someone else who wrote them on paper. But a few times he wrote a small part of the letter himself, as he did here.

I, Paulos, write this with my own hand. I will repay it: Paulos emphasized that he was promising to pay what Onesimos owed to Filemon (Philemon) by writing the promise himself in his own handwriting. Another way of expressing this is like the GNT: “I, Paulos, will pay you back.”

19b

not to mention that you owe me your very self.

  • But don’t forget that you also are in debt to me for your new spiritual life because I helped you to become a Christian.

  • You know already that, if I had not helped you, you would not have found new life yourself, so you owe me your own life.

Paulos may have been smiling in the last part of verse 19. He probably knew that Filemon would not force Onesimos to repay him. He probably would not force Paulos to pay anything, because Filemon owed something to Paulos too.

In the middle of this last sentence in verse 19, Paulos (Paul) stopped referring to what he owed Filemon and started referring to what Filemon owed him. So the BSB uses a dash (—) to set the last part of this sentence apart from the text in the earlier part of the verse.

not to mention: This is a way of saying something that Paulos didn’t really want to say because he knew it might cause Filemon to feel a little ashamed. It was Paulos’s way of reminding Filemon of something Filemon already knew. There are other ways to translate the phrase “not to mention.” For example: “I should not have to remind you, of course,” (RSV), “I won’t mention that” (NLT).

you owe me your very self: Paulos had helped Filemon to become a Christian, and so Filemon owed his new spiritual life, his whole Christian life, to Paulos. This meant that Filemon owed Paulos much more than Onesimos (Onesimus) owed Filemon. Another way to translate the Greek word seauton, “your own self,” is “your very soul.” Here are two alternate ways to translate this whole phrase:

Your debt to me is big because through me you received eternal life.

You owe a lot to me because I helped you believe in Christ.

20a

Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord.

  • So, my brother, please do this kind thing for me because we (dual-incl) belong to the Lord.

  • For the Lord’s sake, my brother, please do for me this thing I am asking.

Yes, brother: Paulos (Paul) was again asking Filemon (Philemon) to welcome Onesimos (Onesimus). See verse 17.

some benefit: Paulos was not asking Filemon to help him in some general way. He wanted Filemon to do a specific thing for him. He wanted him to forgive Onesimos and receive him back. So the meaning is clearer in the CEV: “do this for me” (referring to the favor Paulos asked for in verse 17).

in the Lord: The main idea of this phrase seems to be that Paulos wanted Filemon to think about Paulos’s request as a fellow believer in Christ would. And he wanted Filemon to think of Onesimos as a fellow Christian, not only as a slave. Paulos believed that as Filemon thought like this, he would do what Paulos was asking him to do.

20b

Refresh my heart in Christ.

  • Encourage me by doing this as a fellow believer.

  • Do what I ask because we both belong to Christ.

Refresh my heart: “Cheer me up,” “make me happy,” “set my heart at rest,” “relieve my worry.” Paulos was saying, in other words here, what he already said in verse 20a. He used the same phrase here that he used in verse 7.

in Christ: This is the same kind of phrase as “in the Lord” (20a). Another way to say it is: “as a fellow Christian.”

Verse 20b means the same as verse 20a. Paulos (Paul) was still saying that he wanted Filemon (Philemon) to do what he had asked him to do. Here are two ways to translate it:

Make me happy as a Christian brother by doing this favor for me.

Cause me to be happy as your Christian brother: do this favor for me.

Read verses 17–21 again.

21

This verse is a summary of what Paulos was asking Filemon to do for Onesimos. Paulos believed quite strongly that Filemon would do what he was asking him to do. And Paulos may also have been thinking as he wrote this verse that perhaps Filemon would cancel all of Onesimos’s debt. See notes on verses 19 and 20.

21a

Confident of your obedience, I write to you,

  • Even as I write to you, I am sure you will do what I asked.

confident: Paulos (Paul) meant, “I am sure,” or, “I know.” He was reassuring Filemon (Philemon) that he believed that Filemon would be willing to do what Paulos was asking him to do.

your obedience: The Greek words translated your obedience literally mean “that you will agree to my request.” Paulos had said in verses 8 and 9 that he was asking Filemon to do only what Filemon chose willingly to do. He was not ordering him. The way the CEV translates it is probably closer to the actual meaning: “knowing that you will do what I ask you.”

I write: Paulos himself wrote the part in verse 19 but probably did not write the whole letter with his own hand. He usually had someone write for him while Paulos told him what to write. Paulos was saying here that he was the one who had chosen what words to put in the letter.

21b

knowing that you will do even more than I ask.

  • Yes, I know that you will do even more than I asked.

even more than I ask: Paulos believed that Filemon would do all that was right as a Christian. This meant not only doing what Paulos asked, which was to accept Onesimos (Onesimus) back, but doing more as well. Paulos may have been thinking about two things when he said even more: (a) Perhaps Filemon would not force Onesimos or Paulos to repay any of Onesimos’s debts. And (b) perhaps Filemon would free Onesimos from slavery. But Bible scholars do not know whether Paulos was thinking this, and they don’t know if Filemon did either of these things.

title: Philemon 1:22
content:
Section 22–25: Others greet Filemon (Philemon)

In verses 22–25 Paulos (Paul) wrote to the group of Christians who were with Filemon. So he used “you (plur)” in these verses as he did in verse 3. But in the main Sections of the letter (verses 4–21) he used “you (singular)” rather than “you (plur).” This is one thing that shows that verses 1–3 and verses 22–25 are separate from the other Sections of the letter. So verses 22–25, as a unit, are also a Section that is separate from the other parts of the letter.

After making his main point in the letter in verses 8–21, Paulos finished the letter with a few final words in verses 22–25. He asked Filemon to prepare a guest room for him (verse 22), because he hoped that God would answer the prayers of the Christians at Kolossai (Colosse) by allowing him to visit them again. Then Paulos sent greetings to Filemon from five Christian friends who were there with Paulos (verses 23–24). These peoples’ names are also in Colossians 4:10–14. Finally, Paulos ended the letter with a Christian blessing (verse 25).

Read verses 22–25 carefully in the BSB and the GNT.

Paragraph 22 Paulos asks Filemon to prepare for Paulos to come

In this verse, Paulos asked Filemon to get things ready for Paulos to come and visit Filemon.

Read verse 22 again.

22a

In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me,

  • ¶ And another thing: Please get a room ready in your house for me to stay in,

  • ¶ While I am asking you to do something kind for Onesimos (Onesimus), I ask you to do something else for me. Please prepare a room in your house for me so that I can stay with you as a guest,

In the meantime: You could translate the Greek words here: “At the same time.” For example:

At the same time that I am asking this favor for Onesimos, I will ask another favor for myself.

prepare a guest room for me: Paulos (Paul) was asking Filemon (Philemon) to prepare a place for him to stay at Kolossai (Colosse). This would be a place in Filemon’s house where Paulos could sleep and where Filemon’s servants could cook food for him. Paulos apparently thought that the people who had put him in prison would soon free him from prison.

22b

because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.

  • because I hope that God will answer your(plur) prayers and cause people to release me from prison and let me come and see you(plur) again.

I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you: Paulos was not simply saying that he wanted to go and see Filemon and the Colossian Christians. He was saying that someone else—probably God—would need to cause this to happen.

Here are two examples of a free translation of this part of verse 22:

I hope that God will make a way for me to become free so I can see you again.

I hope that God will cause those who imprisoned me to free me so I can see you again.

I hope: Paulos (Paul) did not say that he was sure the Roman leaders would free him, but he wanted and expected this to happen. Bible scholars do not know whether Paulos ever went to Kolossai (Colosse) again or if he ever saw Filemon (Philemon) again.

through your prayers: Paulos knew that the Christians in Kolossai were praying that he would be able to leave prison. So he was saying that, if he became free, it would be because God had answered their prayers.

restored to you: Paulos hoped that the people who had put him in prison would release him, and that as a result, he would be able to visit the Colossians.

to you: Paulos used you (plur) two times in this verse. So here again he was writing not only to Filemon but also to the Christians at Kolossai who worshipped God in Filemon’s house.

Paragraph 23–24 Fellow believers greet Filemon

In verses 23–24 Paulos sent greetings to Filemon from fellow Christians who were where Paulos was. Consider how you would translate such a greeting into your language.

Read verses 23–24 again.

23

Epafras (Epaphras), my fellow prisoner in Christ Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), sends you greetings,

  • ¶ Epafras greets you. He is in prison with me because he, too, serves Christ Yeshua.

  • ¶ Epafras is a prisoner here with me because he preaches about Yeshua Christ. He greets you.

Epafras: This was a friend of both Filemon (Philemon) and Paulos (Paul). Paulos also wrote about this same Epafras in Colossians 1:7, 4:12.

my fellow prisoner: There are two ideas about what this means:

  1. a man who was in prison with Paulos

  2. a man who had been a prisoner like Paulos was

The first meaning is probably the closest to what Paulos was saying, because Paulos sent greetings from Epafras (Epaphras) to the Colossian Christians. Since Epafras was there with Paulos as his fellow prisoner, it is more likely that he was in prison with Paulos.

in Christ Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus): Both Paulos and Epafras were in prison because of the Good News of Yeshua Christ. Paulos also referred to himself as “a prisoner of Christ Yeshua” in verse 1. Paulos was in prison because many people didn’t want him to continue preaching about Yeshua. Some commentators say that Epafras went into prison so that he could help Paulos. Others say that Epafras was in prison because he also preached the Good News, and the phrase “my fellow prisoner” seems to imply this.

sends you greetings: Epafras and the others whose names are in verse 24 asked Paulos to send their greetings to their friend Filemon. The you (singular) means that these friends were greeting Filemon as an individual person. It was their way of reminding Filemon that they still loved him and thought well of him.

Read verses 23–24 again.

24

as do Markos (Mark), Aristarkos (Aristarchus), Demas, and Lukas (Luke), my fellow workers.

  • And others here who help me as I work to proclaim the Gospel—Markos, Aristarkos, Demas and Lukas—they also greet you.

as do: This means “these others also send you greetings.”

Markos: This was Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos, the Jewish Christian who wrote the Gospel of Markos. (Acts 12:25).

Aristarkos: Another Jewish Christian who was there with Paulos (Paul) was Aristarkos. His hometown was Thessalonikai (Thessalonica). (Acts 19:29).

Demas: Demas was a Gentile Christian, not a Yehudi (Jew). Bible scholars don’t know if this was the same Demas who later left Paulos (2 Timothy 4:10).

Lukas: This was the same Lukas who wrote the Gospel of Lukas and the Acts of the Apostles. He was a Gentile Christian and a medical doctor (Colossians 4:14).

my fellow workers: These four men were working together with Paulos, helping him in various ways to help people know about the Good News (see verse 1). Notice that Paulos did not say they were his “fellow prisoners,” as he said about Epafras (Epaphras) (verse 23). These four men were free to continue working with Paulos to spread the Gospel, even though he himself was in prison.

Paragraph 25 Good-bye

Read verse 25 again.

25

The grace of the Lord Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ be with your spirit.

  • ¶ May our(incl) Lord Yeshua Christ bless you all.

grace: See notes on verse 3. Paulos said again that he wanted the Lord to help and bless Paulos’s fellow Christians at Kolossai, and he prayed for this. Verse 25 shows the way Paulos ended many of his letters. (See 1 Corinthians 16:23, Colossians 4:18, 1 Thessalonians 5:28.)

be with your spirit: This does not refer to some spirit that was separate from the Christians Paulos was writing to. He was talking about the people themselves. It is another way of saying “be with you.” The word your is plural and shows that Paulos wanted this grace or blessing to be with all the Christians at Kolossai. Also the word spirit is singular (meaning “one spirit”). Paulos was writing to them as one group of God’s united people.
